premise: Fictional patients. Item numbers checked against MBS Online, Services Australia, Health, AskMBS, RACGP and legislation sources. No dollar figures: fees are indexed (most rose 2.6% on 1 July 2026), so check the current fee on MBS Online.

rules.text: Level A (3): short, obvious, straightforward problem. Level B (23): at least 6 and under 20 minutes. Level C (36): 20 to under 40. Level D (44): 40 to under 60. Level E (123): 60 minutes or more.

sources.t: Legislation: Level B 'at least 6 minutes' (from 1 Nov 2023)

rules.text: Count active attention on the patient, including extra time to communicate (interpreter, hearing or speech difficulty, dementia) and My Health Record work while the patient is present.
Don't count notes, forms, referrals or uploads after the patient leaves, or talking with relatives while the patient is absent.
A continuation of the same attendance is billed as one item. Time can't be banked toward two services.
Non-urgent attendances spanning in-hours and after-hours: the period with the greater portion decides the item type.
Urgent after-hours items need a genuinely urgent assessment. PSR has reviewed these items.
From 1 Nov 2025, bulk billing incentives (Group M1) apply to all Medicare-eligible patients, not just under-16s and concession card holders.

sources.t: MBS Online: BBI changes from 1 Nov 2025

rules.text: Triple incentive: items 23, 36, 44, 123 face to face, 91800 video and 91891 phone; plus 91801, 91802, 91920, 91900 and 91910 for MyMedicare-enrolled patients. Other unreferred services (incl. Level A and antenatal) get the single incentive.

rules.text: MBS Online's MMM1 examples: 23 + 75870; 91900 + 75880 (MyMedicare); 91801 + 10990 (not MyMedicare). Incentive item numbers vary with the Modified Monash category.
Split billing is allowed (e.g. bulk-billed 23 for a second issue, privately billed 30071), but two Group T8 surgical items must be billed the same way.
MBS telehealth needs MyMedicare registration with your practice, or a face-to-face service at your practice in the last 12 months. Prior phone or video consults don't count.

Exemptions include under-12-month-olds, homelessness, BBV/sexual and reproductive health, AMS/ACCHS services and urgent after-hours. Mental health plan items lost their exemption on 1 Nov 2025 (FPS kept it).
Level C and D phone items (91900, 91910) are for MyMedicare-registered patients only.

rules.text: 701: 30 min or less; 703: over 30 to under 45; 705: 45 to under 60; 707: 60+. A practice nurse can assist.
45–49 at risk: once only. 75+: annually. A second assessment in 12 months needs a different target group, stated on the claim.
Heart health check (699): once in 12 months; not after another health assessment in the last 12 months (Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander assessments excepted).
715: not within 9 months of a 715, 228, 92004 or 92011. Follow-up allied health (81300–81360): up to 10 a calendar year.
16500 + 23 on the same day only for two distinct services (e.g. an unrelated intercurrent problem), with separate times recorded. All pregnancy care: 16500 only.
Antenatal attendances get the single bulk billing incentive, not the triple.
Procedure items are complete services: consent, routine pre/post-op care and advice are included. Add an attendance only for work beyond that or a separate, distinct issue.
Routine post-operative care by the proceduralist is included in skin procedure items.

sources.t: Services Australia: skin lesion and biopsy billing

rules.text: 30071: diagnostic skin biopsy, independent procedure, specimen to pathology. 30026: superficial wound repair, not face or neck, up to 7 cm.
30192: ablative treatment of 10 or more premalignant lesions. Fewer than 10 solar keratoses are covered by the attendance item.

sources.t: Services Australia: skin lesion and biopsy billing

rules.text: 35501: 40% loading on 35503, 35506, 14206 or 30062 when the LARC service is bulk billed (from 1 Nov 2025).
Vitamin D (66833) only for listed indications (e.g. osteoporosis/osteomalacia signs, raised ALP with normal LFTs, malabsorption, deeply pigmented skin or severe lack of sun, anticonvulsants, CKD).
B12 (66838): once in 12 months; holoTC/MMA (66839) if B12 low or equivocal. Folate (66840): at-risk patients only.

sources.t: NPS RADAR: B12, folate and vitamin D items

rules.text: HbA1c: monitoring established diabetes (66551) up to 4 in 12 months; diagnosis in asymptomatic high-risk patients (66841) once in 12 months.
PSA (66655): once in 23 months. First-degree family history (66654): once in 11 months.
TSH (66716) first; free T4/T3 (66719) only if TSH is abnormal or a listed indication applies.

Standard lipid items have no frequency cap in the descriptor; lipoprotein electrophoresis (66539) is twice in 12 months. Iron studies (66596) and coeliac serology (71163 one antibody, 71164 two or more) have no descriptor cap.
80/20 rule: 80+ relevant services on each of 20+ days in 12 months is deemed inappropriate practice (30/20 for phone). Leads to PSR referral.
PSR findings include unmet time requirements, same-day co-claiming workarounds, thin care plans and services without clinical indication.

scenarios.consult: Kim, 45. Sore ear for three days. History, otoscopy, a plan and safety-netting. 12 minutes face to face, in your rooms.
scenarios.why: Level B is at least 6 and less than 20 minutes. Twelve minutes sits squarely in it. Level A is for the short, obvious, straightforward problem.
scenarios.risk: Level A under-claims a genuine Level B. Level C claims eight minutes that never happened, and PSR has found time requirements not met for items 23, 36 and 44.

sources.t: Legislation: Level B 'at least 6 minutes' (from 1 Nov 2023)

scenarios.consult: Mrs Ali, 81. A long consult with lots going on. Afterwards you also did some admin and spoke to her daughter.
scenarios.q: Which of these count toward the time tier? (Pick all that apply.)
options: Examining her and talking through the plan
Updating her My Health Record while she's still in the room
Writing your notes and a referral after she's left
Ten minutes with her daughter in the corridor while Mrs Ali is in the bathroom
Extra time needed to work through a phone interpreter
scenarios.why: Only active attention on the patient counts, including the extra time it genuinely takes to communicate (interpreter, hearing loss, dementia). My Health Record work counts while the patient is present. Notes, forms and referrals after they've left don't, and neither does talking to a relative while the patient is absent.
scenarios.risk: Padding the clock with paperwork is how a Level B becomes an over-claimed Level C. Leaving out interpreter time is the opposite mistake: legitimate minutes left on the table.

scenarios.consult: Mrs Tran, 62. New diabetes diagnosis, via a TIS phone interpreter. 24 minutes face to face; the same consult in English would have taken about 15.
options: Level B (item 23): bill what it 'would' have taken
Level B plus a separate interpreter item
scenarios.why: Extra time needed to communicate effectively counts, interpreters included. Twenty-four minutes of active attention is Level C. Note the reason for the extra time, and the TIS job number, in your notes.
scenarios.risk: Billing Level B quietly penalises you for doing the right thing. There's no separate interpreter item to add.

scenarios.consult: Mr Okafor, 68. Five chronic problems, a medication review and a frank talk about prognosis. 62 minutes of continuous face-to-face time.
options: Level D (44) plus a Level B (23) for the overflow
scenarios.why: Level E (item 123) is for 60 minutes or more. One continuous attendance is one item: you can't split it into two to make the maths work.
scenarios.risk: Splitting one attendance into two items is billing the same time twice. Under-calling it as Level D leaves the Level E difference behind.

scenarios.consult: Lou, 55. You see him for 14 minutes, he leaves, then pops back five minutes later because you both forgot to recheck his blood pressure. Same problem, same plan.
options: Two: a Level B (23) and a Level A (3)
None for the second bit, but add a bulk billing incentive twice
scenarios.why: When the second contact is a continuation of the first attendance, you bill one time-based attendance item. Time used for one service can't be banked toward another.
scenarios.risk: Two items for one continuous episode is exactly the duplication auditors look for.

scenarios.consult: Jordan, 34. No concession card. 15-minute consult for a viral illness, bulk billed. Your practice is in a Modified Monash 1 area. It's November 2026.
options: Item 23 only: incentives are for kids and concession card holders
scenarios.why: From 1 November 2025, bulk billing incentives apply to every Medicare-eligible patient. MBS Online's own example: an MMM1 patient, item 23 bulk billed, plus 75870. The exact incentive item depends on your practice's Modified Monash category.
scenarios.risk: Skipping the incentive on an eligible bulk-billed consult leaves money on the table every single time.

sources.t: MBS Online: BBI changes from 1 Nov 2025

scenarios.consult: Vinnie, 16. Simple script renewal, bulk billed as a Level A (item 3). MMM1 practice.
options: No incentive: Level A doesn't qualify
scenarios.why: The tripled incentive is for the common consults: items 23, 36, 44 and 123 face to face (plus some telehealth items). Level A gets the single incentive; MBS Online's example pairs item 3 with a single incentive. In MMM1 that's 10990.
scenarios.risk: Claiming the triple on a Level A is an over-claim. Claiming nothing is a free incentive walking out the door.

sources.t: RACGP: MBS mental health item changes for GPs

scenarios.consult: Jenny, 40. 35-minute video consult, bulk billed. Not registered in MyMedicare. You saw her face to face seven months ago. MMM1 practice.
options: Nothing: she's not in MyMedicare, so no telehealth
scenarios.why: She's eligible for telehealth because she had a face-to-face service with you in the last 12 months. But the triple incentive on Level C video (91801) needs MyMedicare enrolment, so it's the single incentive, 10990. This is MBS Online's own worked example.
scenarios.risk: Item 36 is a face-to-face item; billing it for video is simply wrong. The triple incentive here would be an over-claim.

sources.t: RACGP: MBS mental health item changes for GPs

scenarios.consult: Paul, 52. 25-minute phone consult, bulk billed. Registered in MyMedicare with your practice. MMM1.
scenarios.why: Level C by phone is 91900, and it's only available to MyMedicare-registered patients. Bulk billed and enrolled, it attracts the triple incentive, 75880. Straight out of MBS Online's scenarios.
scenarios.risk: 91891 is the Level B phone item: under-claiming 25 minutes. 91801 is video, and 36 is face to face.

sources.t: RACGP: MBS mental health item changes for GPs

scenarios.consult: Ravi, 60. You bulk bill a Level B (item 23) for his blood pressure, and he'd like a skin biopsy (30071) of a separate lesion done today. Your practice charges privately for procedures.
scenarios.q: Can you bulk bill the 23 and privately bill the 30071?
options: No: one patient, one day, one billing method
Yes: split billing like this is allowed
Only if you drop the biopsy item
Yes, and you can also privately bill the 23
scenarios.why: Split billing is permitted, unless billing one item affects the fee for another. A bulk-billed time-tiered attendance for a second issue plus a privately billed biopsy is fine. Two Group T8 surgical items on the same occasion, though, must both be bulk billed or both privately billed.
scenarios.risk: Getting this wrong usually means needlessly bulk billing the procedure, or splitting two surgical items, which isn't allowed.

scenarios.consult: Non-urgent consult in your rooms. It starts shortly before the after-hours period begins and runs well into it: most of the time falls after hours.
options: The in-hours item: it started in hours
The after-hours item for that level
Split it: an in-hours item plus an after-hours item
scenarios.why: For non-urgent attendances, the period containing the greater portion of the attendance decides the item type. One attendance, one item.
scenarios.risk: Splitting it is double billing; jumping to an urgent item is a PSR favourite (see the next one).

scenarios.consult: Late in the evening, a patient asks for a repeat of a stable long-term medicine. No new symptoms. Nothing that couldn't wait until morning.
scenarios.q: Is an urgent after-hours attendance item appropriate?
options: No: urgent items need a genuinely urgent assessment
Yes, if you see them by video
scenarios.why: Urgent after-hours items are for patients who genuinely need urgent assessment. PSR has reviewed after-hours and urgent items where an urgent assessment wasn't required.
scenarios.risk: PSR outcomes have included repayments and disqualification from items. A non-urgent after-hours item (or a morning appointment) fits.

scenarios.consult: Sasha, 29. Not registered in MyMedicare. Last face-to-face visit at your practice was 14 months ago; since then, three phone consults. Today she wants a video consult about a new rash. No exemption applies.
scenarios.q: Can you bill an MBS video item?
options: Yes: the phone consults keep the relationship current
No: no face-to-face service in the last 12 months and not MyMedicare-registered
Yes, if you bulk bill it
Yes, as long as it's under 20 minutes
scenarios.why: MBS telehealth needs either MyMedicare registration with your practice, or a face-to-face service at your practice in the last 12 months. Prior video or phone consults don't count as face to face.
scenarios.risk: A non-claimable service billed to Medicare can be recovered. Book her in face to face (or register her in MyMedicare if she's eligible).

scenarios.consult: None of these patients is MyMedicare-registered, and none has had a face-to-face visit with your practice in the last 12 months.
scenarios.q: Who can still get an MBS video consult from you? (Pick all that apply.)
options: A patient wanting a sexual and reproductive health consult
An immunocompromised patient with a chronic condition
A patient wanting a new mental health treatment plan
scenarios.why: Exemptions include patients under 12 months, people experiencing homelessness, and blood-borne virus, sexual or reproductive health consults (among others; record the exemption in your notes). Being immunocompromised isn't an exemption. And since 1 November 2025, mental health plan telehealth items are no longer exempt.
scenarios.risk: Assuming an exemption that doesn't exist is how telehealth claims end up being recovered.

sources.t: RACGP: MBS mental health item changes for GPs

scenarios.consult: Barry, 66, is booked for his GP chronic condition management plan. While he's there, you also sort out a sinus infection. The plan is fully prepared today.
scenarios.why: GPCCMP preparation and review items can't be co-claimed with general attendance items on the same day. Item 965 is a complete service and the only item to claim. If a consult reveals the need for a plan, you can bill the consult and do the plan another day.
scenarios.risk: Billing the 23 on a different day to dodge the rule is exactly what a PSR committee found was inappropriate practice.

sources.t: MBS Online: GP chronic condition management plans

scenarios.consult: Helen, 58, has type 2 diabetes and a GPCCMP. It's clinically relevant to review it regularly.
scenarios.q: How often can the review item (967) be claimed?
scenarios.why: From 1 July 2025: prepare a GPCCMP (965) once every 12 months, and review (967) every 3 months, if clinically relevant (unless exceptional circumstances apply).
scenarios.risk: Reviewing less often than you could, when it's clinically useful, is legitimate income (and care) left behind. More often than allowed gets rejected.

sources.t: MBS Online: GP chronic condition management plans

scenarios.consult: Doug, 71. GPCCMP prepared 20 months ago and never reviewed. He wants a podiatry referral.
options: A review (or new plan): it must have been prepared or reviewed in the last 18 months
scenarios.why: GPCCMPs don't expire, but to keep accessing allied health under the plan, it must have been prepared or reviewed in the previous 18 months. Then it's up to 5 individual allied health services per calendar year (10 for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander patients).
scenarios.risk: A referral built on a stale plan means the podiatry claims can fail, and that lands on the patient.

sources.t: MBS Online: GP chronic condition management plans

scenarios.consult: Priscilla, 63, is registered in MyMedicare with another practice. She's visiting you and asks for a GPCCMP.
options: No: MyMedicare-registered patients access GPCCMP items through their registered practice
scenarios.why: Registered patients access GPCCMP items through their MyMedicare practice; non-registered patients through their usual GP. That applies face to face and by telehealth.
scenarios.risk: The claim won't stand, and it fragments her care.

sources.t: MBS Online: GP chronic condition management plans

scenarios.consult: Frank, 74, has a GP Management Plan and Team Care Arrangements from May 2025. They're due for review.
scenarios.why: GPMP and TCA items (including the 732 review) ceased on 1 July 2025. A patient with an old plan who needs a review moves to the new framework by having a GPCCMP prepared.
scenarios.risk: Ceased items won't pay. Billing 967 reviews a plan that doesn't exist yet.

sources.t: MBS Online: GP chronic condition management plans

scenarios.consult: Your practice nurse spends 30 minutes gathering history and measurements to help you draft Rosa's brand-new GPCCMP.
scenarios.q: Can the nurse's time be billed as 10997?
options: Yes: 10997 covers any nurse time for a plan
No: 10997 can't be used to help prepare a plan
Yes, up to 10 times a year
scenarios.why: Item 10997 is for ongoing monitoring and support between reviews for patients with a GPCCMP (up to 5 per calendar year), not for preparing the plan. The plan item (965) is a complete service.
scenarios.risk: Using 10997 for plan prep double-bills the same work.

sources.t: MBS Online: GP chronic condition management plans

scenarios.consult: Ella, 31, back after six psychology sessions. 22-minute review of her mental health treatment plan, face to face. It's November 2026, and you're her usual GP.
options: 36 (Level C), noting it's an MHTP review
scenarios.why: Items 2712 and 2713 were removed on 1 November 2025. Reviews and ongoing mental health consults now use the time-tiered items: 22 minutes is Level C. Document that it's a plan review. Bulk billed, item 36 attracts the triple incentive.
scenarios.risk: Removed items get rejected. Use the time tier, and longer consults pay accordingly.

sources.t: RACGP: MBS mental health item changes for GPs
MBS Online: Better Access changes for GPs

scenarios.consult: Tom, 27. You prepare his mental health treatment plan face to face in 35 minutes. You haven't done mental health skills training.
scenarios.why: Without mental health skills training: 2700 (20 to under 40 minutes) or 2701 (40+). With training: 2715 and 2717 for the same tiers.
scenarios.risk: Claiming the training items without the training is an over-claim. Calling it 2701 claims time you didn't spend.

sources.t: RACGP: MBS mental health item changes for GPs

scenarios.consult: Noor, 22. New to your practice, not registered in MyMedicare anywhere. She's moved to town and plans to see you for her care from now on. She needs a mental health treatment plan.
scenarios.q: Can you prepare and bill the MHTP?
options: No: she must be MyMedicare-registered first
Yes: you can be her usual medical practitioner; document that
Only if you've seen her for 12 months
scenarios.why: From 1 November 2025, MHTPs come from the patient's MyMedicare practice or their usual medical practitioner. That includes a GP likely to provide most of their care over the next 12 months. If you haven't seen them before, record that the patient told you you're their usual practitioner.
scenarios.risk: Turning her away loses a legitimate service. Billing it for a one-off walk-in who has a usual GP elsewhere doesn't meet the rule.

sources.t: RACGP: MBS mental health item changes for GPs
MBS Online: Better Access changes for GPs

scenarios.consult: Gwen, 79. Her annual 75+ health assessment. Your practice nurse and you together spend 50 minutes on it.
scenarios.why: Health assessment tiers: 701 is 30 minutes or less, 703 more than 30 and under 45, 705 at least 45 and under 60, 707 is 60 or more. A practice nurse can assist, and the GP chooses the item considering total time and complexity.
scenarios.risk: Calling a 50-minute assessment 'standard' under-claims; 'prolonged' over-claims.

scenarios.consult: Lena, 48. Had the 45–49 'at risk of chronic disease' health assessment at 46. She asks for it again.
scenarios.why: The 45–49 health assessment is once only. The 75+ assessment is annual. A second health assessment in the same 12 months is only possible under a different target group, and the claim must say which.
scenarios.risk: Repeating a once-only item gets rejected. Check if she's eligible under another target group instead.

scenarios.consult: Jim, 47. Had his 45–49 health assessment five months ago. Today he asks for a heart health check (699) as well.
options: No: 699 can't follow another health assessment within 12 months (Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander assessments aside)
scenarios.why: The heart health check is once in 12 months and can't be claimed if the patient has had a health assessment in the previous 12 months, except Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander health assessments. On the same day, it's only OK if the other assessment is done after the heart health check.
scenarios.risk: The claim gets knocked back, or worse, gets paid and later recovered.

scenarios.consult: Darren, 38, is Aboriginal. His 715 health assessment was eight months ago, and it identified a need for physio and dietetics follow-up.
scenarios.q: Which is correct? (Pick all that apply.)
options: 715 isn't claimable within 9 months of a 715, 228, 92004 or 92011
Follow-up allied health items (81300–81360) are capped at 10 services per calendar year, combined
Follow-up allied health is capped at 5 per year
scenarios.why: Item 715 needs 9 months since the last Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander health assessment (715, 228, 92004 or 92011). When it identifies a need, follow-up allied health items are available, up to 10 services per calendar year combined.
scenarios.risk: A 715 claimed a month early gets rejected. Missing the follow-up items leaves the patient (and the plan) under-served. PSR has also reviewed 715s for clinical indication and records, so do the whole thing.

scenarios.consult: Ana, 29, at 24 weeks. Routine antenatal visit: BP, fundal height, results. She also rolled her ankle at netball, and you assess and manage it. You record separate times for each.
scenarios.why: Co-claiming 16500 and 23 is permissible when you provide two distinct, clinically relevant services: the antenatal visit and an unrelated intercurrent problem. Document the separate problem and times. You can't use 23 to cover pregnancy-related work.
scenarios.risk: Billing 16500 alone leaves the ankle unbilled. Billing 36 for both misdescribes the antenatal care.

scenarios.consult: Bea, 31, at 30 weeks. 18 minutes: BP, fundal height, fetal movements, and a chat about pregnancy reflux and sleep. Nothing unrelated to the pregnancy.
scenarios.why: If the whole encounter is pregnancy care, it's 16500 only. Pregnancy-related issues within the antenatal visit aren't a separate 23.
scenarios.risk: Adding a 23 for pregnancy-related work is the co-claiming error PSR has flagged in obstetric cases.

scenarios.consult: Cate, 26. Routine antenatal visit (16500), bulk billed, MMM1 practice.
scenarios.why: Tripled incentives weren't extended to antenatal visits. For incentive purposes they're 'other unreferred services', so the single incentive applies (10990 in MMM1).
scenarios.risk: Triple is an over-claim; nothing leaves the single incentive on the table.

scenarios.consult: Merv, 74. You treat 14 solar keratoses on his forearms and scalp with cryotherapy.
scenarios.q: What do you bill for the cryotherapy?
options: Nothing extra: it's part of the consult
scenarios.why: Item 30192 covers ablative treatment of premalignant skin lesions, 10 or more. Fewer than 10 solar keratoses are covered by the attendance item instead.
scenarios.risk: Fourteen lesions billed as just a consult is a procedure left unbilled. Biopsy and wound items don't apply to cryotherapy.

sources.t: Services Australia: skin lesion and biopsy billing

scenarios.consult: Same as Merv, but this time six solar keratoses, frozen during a consult.
scenarios.why: Fewer than 10 solar keratoses treated ablatively are covered by attendance items. 30192 starts at 10.
scenarios.risk: Billing 30192 for six lesions is an over-claim that's easy to detect.

sources.t: Services Australia: skin lesion and biopsy billing

scenarios.consult: Mary, 66. 30-minute check-up and script review. While taking her BP, you spot a suspicious lesion on her arm and do a punch biopsy, sent to pathology.
scenarios.why: A genuine 30-minute consult plus a separate diagnostic biopsy sent for histology: both items. This is MBS Online's own worked example. 30071 needs the specimen sent for pathological examination.
scenarios.risk: Dropping the biopsy item leaves a procedure unbilled. The attendance time should be the consult, not the biopsy minutes.

scenarios.consult: Theo, 30. Walk-in with a 5 cm superficial cut on his forearm from a broken glass. You assess it, get consent, close it and give wound-care advice. Nothing else is discussed.
scenarios.why: Procedure items are complete services: consent, routine pre- and post-procedure care and advice are included. 30026 covers a superficial wound repair, not on the face or neck, up to 7 cm. Add an attendance only if you go beyond the routine, or deal with a separate, distinct problem.
scenarios.risk: Adding a 23 for work already included in the procedure is the classic co-claim trap.

scenarios.consult: A week after you excised a lesion from Pat's back, he's in for suture removal and a wound check. All healing nicely.
options: Nothing: routine aftercare is part of the procedure item
scenarios.why: Skin procedure items include professional attendances for routine post-operative care by the practitioner who did the procedure, through to the final check.
scenarios.risk: A 23 for routine aftercare you've already been paid for is an over-claim.

sources.t: Services Australia: skin lesion and biopsy billing

scenarios.consult: Everything here is bulk billed, from 1 November 2025.
scenarios.q: Which pairs are valid? (Pick all that apply.)
scenarios.why: Item 35501 is a loading of 40% of the LARC item fee (35503, 35506, 14206 or 30062) when the LARC service, and the other items for it, are bulk billed. It doesn't attach to private billing or non-LARC procedures.
scenarios.risk: Forgetting 35501 on a bulk-billed IUD or implant leaves 40% of the procedure fee behind.

scenarios.consult: You're ordering 25-hydroxyvitamin D for several patients.
scenarios.q: Which requests meet the Medicare criteria for item 66833? (Pick all that apply.)
options: Office worker, tired, wants 'a vitamin D check'
Raised ALP with otherwise normal liver tests
scenarios.why: The lab bills these, not you; your request decides whether Medicare pays. 66833 is only for listed indications: e.g. signs of osteoporosis or osteomalacia; raised ALP with otherwise normal LFTs; hyperparathyroidism or calcium/phosphate problems; malabsorption; deeply pigmented skin or chronic severe lack of sun; medicines that lower vitamin D (like anticonvulsants); chronic kidney failure; and some children and infants. Tiredness and 'just checking' aren't on the list.
scenarios.risk: Outside the criteria there's no rebate, so the patient may get a bill. Write the indication on the request.

sources.t: NPS RADAR: B12, folate and vitamin D items

scenarios.consult: Wayne, 60, has type 2 diabetes. He's already had four HbA1c tests in the last 12 months and asks for another 'just to see'.
options: No: monitoring HbA1c (66551) is capped at 4 in 12 months
scenarios.why: The lab bills these, not you; your request decides whether Medicare pays. HbA1c for managing established diabetes (66551) can't be claimed more than 4 times in 12 months. Pregnancy with pre-existing diabetes has its own item (66554, up to 6 in 12 months).
scenarios.risk: Relabelling it as 'diagnosis' to get it paid is misrepresenting the request.

scenarios.consult: Kerry, 47, asymptomatic, high risk for diabetes. Her diagnostic HbA1c seven months ago was normal. She'd like another.
scenarios.q: Is a repeat diagnostic HbA1c rebated today?
options: No: diagnostic HbA1c (66841) is once in 12 months
scenarios.why: The lab bills these, not you; your request decides whether Medicare pays. 66841 is HbA1c for diagnosis in asymptomatic patients at high risk: once in 12 months. The monitoring item (66551) is only for established diabetes.
scenarios.risk: Ordering it under the 'established diabetes' item when she doesn't have diabetes is a misdescribed request.

scenarios.consult: Two asymptomatic men want a PSA. Geoff, 58, no family history, had one 14 months ago. Phil, 55, whose brother has prostate cancer, had one 12 months ago.
scenarios.q: Which is right? (Pick all that apply.)
options: Geoff's repeat isn't rebated yet: 66655 is once in 23 months
Geoff's repeat is fine: PSA is yearly
Phil's repeat is rebated: the first-degree family history item (66654) is once in 11 months
Phil has to wait 23 months too
scenarios.why: The lab bills these, not you; your request decides whether Medicare pays. Since 1 November 2023, the general PSA item 66655 is once in 23 months. Men with a first-degree relative with prostate cancer have 66654, once in 11 months.
scenarios.risk: Too early on 66655 and the patient may get a bill. Using 66655 for Phil makes him wait unnecessarily.

scenarios.consult: Lily, 30, tired, no thyroid history, not on thyroid-affecting medicines. You'd like to check her thyroid.
options: TSH, free T4 and free T3, all upfront
TSH first; free T4/T3 rebated (66719) only if the TSH is abnormal or a listed indication applies
Nothing: thyroid tests need a specialist
scenarios.why: The lab bills these, not you; your request decides whether Medicare pays. TSH alone is 66716. Free T4 and/or T3 are added under 66719 if the TSH is out of range, or for listed indications such as monitoring thyroid disease, dementia or psychiatric illness, amenorrhoea or infertility, suspected pituitary problems, or drugs that affect thyroid function.
scenarios.risk: The full panel 'just because' isn't how the item works. Let the lab cascade.

scenarios.consult: A few B12 and folate requests land on your desk.
scenarios.q: Which are rebated? (Pick all that apply.)
options: Repeat serum B12, six months after a normal one
Serum folate in a patient with coeliac disease
HoloTC (66839) after an equivocal serum B12
scenarios.why: The lab bills these, not you; your request decides whether Medicare pays. Serum B12 (66838) is once in 12 months. B12 markers like holoTC (66839) are for a low or equivocal serum B12. Folate (66840) is for patients at risk of deficiency, e.g. malabsorption, macrocytic anaemia or coeliac disease.
scenarios.risk: Unrebated tests can mean a surprise bill for the patient.

sources.t: NPS RADAR: B12, folate and vitamin D items

scenarios.consult: Gordon, 67, started a statin three months ago. You want repeat lipids to check his response.
scenarios.q: Does the MBS cap how often standard lipid tests are rebated?
options: No frequency cap in the standard lipid item descriptors; lipoprotein electrophoresis (66539) is the capped one (twice in 12 months)
Yes: twice in 12 months for everything
scenarios.why: The lab bills these, not you; your request decides whether Medicare pays. The standard chemistry items that cover cholesterol, triglycerides and HDL don't carry a frequency limit in the descriptor. The capped lipid item is lipoprotein electrophoresis (66539, twice in 12 months). The limit that matters is clinical: test when it changes management.
scenarios.risk: No rebate cap isn't a licence to over-test: repeated unnecessary tests are a classic over-servicing pattern.

scenarios.consult: A locum is proud of his 'efficiency': 85 or more attendances on most days over the past year.
options: 80% of patients must be bulk billed on 20 days
80 or more relevant attendance services on each of 20 or more days in 12 months is deemed inappropriate practice (barring exceptional circumstances)
No more than 80 patients a week
scenarios.why: Rendering or initiating 80 or more relevant services on each of 20 or more days in 12 months is a prescribed pattern of services. The count runs across all provider numbers and locations. There's a 30/20 rule for phone services too.
scenarios.risk: A breach leads to referral to the Director of Professional Services Review.

scenarios.consult: Lina, 58, MMM1 practice. A 15-minute consult for her reflux (23), then a punch biopsy of a separate lesion (30071). Everything bulk billed.
options: One incentive per patient per day: 75870 only
scenarios.why: Each bulk-billed unreferred service attracts its incentive. Level B gets the triple (75870 in MMM1). A procedure gets the single (10990 in MMM1). MBS Online's own scenario does exactly this, same day.
scenarios.risk: Missing the procedure's incentive leaves money behind. Tripling the procedure is an over-claim.

sources.t: MBS Online: Supporting bulk billing in general practice factsheet

scenarios.consult: Saturday 4 pm, non-urgent. Ollie, 8, earache. 14 minutes, after-hours Level B (5020), bulk billed, MMM1.
options: Triple (75870): after-hours equivalents of Levels B to E get the triple
scenarios.why: The triple incentive covers Levels B to E including out-of-rooms, aged care and after-hours equivalents.
scenarios.risk: Single is under-claiming. Both is double-dipping.

sources.t: MBS Online: Supporting bulk billing in general practice factsheet
MBS Online: BBI changes factsheet (1 Nov 2025)

scenarios.consult: You visit an aged care home in business hours and see three residents, all bulk billed.
scenarios.q: Which are right? (Pick all that apply.)
options: 90001 with the first resident's attendance only
An incentive on each resident's attendance
scenarios.why: The flag-fall is once per facility visit, billed with the first patient's attendance, and billed the same way as that attendance. Incentives apply to attendance items, not the flag-fall. No flag-fall with after-hours, urgent after-hours or telehealth.
scenarios.risk: Three flag-falls for one trip is the kind of pattern that gets a letter.

scenarios.consult: Freya, 24, has a hormonal IUD inserted. You bulk bill 35503 + 35501. The practice wants to add a 'consumables fee' on top.
options: No: a bulk-billed service is paid in full by the benefit
Yes, if it's on a separate invoice
Only if she agrees in writing
scenarios.why: When you bulk bill, you accept the Medicare benefit as full payment. No extra charge can be raised for any reason. If you want to charge, privately bill (and then 35501 doesn't apply).
scenarios.risk: A gap on a bulk-billed claim is a compliance problem, not an admin quirk.

scenarios.consult: You're about to do a skin biopsy (30071).
scenarios.q: Which would justify billing an attendance as well? (Pick all that apply.)
options: Discussing results and management options for a lesion
scenarios.why: Procedure items include the interactions reasonably needed to do them: consent, routine pre- and post-procedure care, routine aftercare. Work that goes beyond that, like discussing results and management options, or a separate issue, can earn an attendance.
scenarios.risk: Billing a 23 for consent and wound advice is unbundling. Skipping the 23 when you genuinely did more is a donation.

scenarios.consult: Hal, 70. Blocked ears. History, otoscopy, syringing both ears, re-check. 24 minutes with him.
scenarios.why: Uncomplicated wax removal, by syringing or microsuction, is part of the general attendance, and the time counts. 24 minutes is Level C. 41500 is for a foreign body, not wax.
scenarios.risk: 41500 for wax is an invalid item. Level A undersells 24 minutes of work.

scenarios.consult: Foreign body day at the clinic.
scenarios.q: Which item-to-job matches are right? (Pick all that apply.)
options: 41500: bead in the ear, removed with a hook (not syringing)
41659: bean up the nose, not removable by simple probing
42644: embedded corneal metal fragment, completely removed
30064 for a splinter flicked out with a needle, no incision
scenarios.why: 41500: ear foreign body, other than by simple syringing. 41659: nose foreign body, other than by simple probing. 42644: complete removal of an embedded corneal or scleral foreign body. 30064 needs incision and exploration.
scenarios.risk: Using a procedure item for wax or a needle flick claims a procedure you didn't do.

scenarios.consult: Dan, 41, angle grinder. You completely remove an embedded corneal fragment, then find and remove a second one in the same eye, same visit.
options: One: not more than once on the same day by the same practitioner
scenarios.why: 42644 is limited to once on the same day by the same practitioner.
scenarios.risk: A second 42644 gets rejected, or paid and later recovered.

scenarios.consult: Mia, 19. Glass in the sole of her foot. Local anaesthetic, incision, exploration, fragment out, two sutures.
scenarios.why: 30064 covers removal of a subcutaneous foreign body needing incision and exploration, including closure of the wound if performed.
scenarios.risk: Adding a wound repair item for the closure double-bills the same wound.

scenarios.consult: Kit, 6, fell off the monkey bars. 2 cm superficial laceration on the chin, closed with sutures. Nothing else.
scenarios.why: Face or neck, up to 7 cm, superficial: 30032. Deeper tissue on the face or neck would be 30035. 30026 and 30029 are for wounds not on the face or neck.
scenarios.risk: The wrong site group is an item mismatch any claims audit spots.

scenarios.consult: Joel, 35. 6 cm forearm laceration from a box cutter, through to subcutaneous fat and fascia, layered closure.
scenarios.why: Not face or neck, up to 7 cm, involving deeper tissue: 30029. Superficial would be 30026.
scenarios.risk: Calling a layered repair 30026 under-claims. Calling it a face repair is just wrong.

scenarios.consult: Theo, 30, has a 5 cm superficial forearm cut repaired (30026). He also asks you to review his blood pressure readings and medication: 10 minutes, separately recorded.
scenarios.why: The repair is its own complete service. The blood pressure review is a separate, distinct problem, so an attendance is legitimate. Count only the BP minutes toward the tier.
scenarios.risk: Leaving off the 23 under-claims genuine work. Folding the procedure into a 36 banks procedure minutes into a time tier.

scenarios.consult: Two days after you drained Dean's back abscess (30219), he's back for packing removal and a dressing.
options: Nothing: aftercare is in the procedure fee
scenarios.why: 30219 is described as 'excluding aftercare'. For items like that, you bill attendance items for the aftercare.
scenarios.risk: Treating it like other skin items leaves the follow-up unbilled. Billing 30219 twice is a procedure that didn't happen.

sources.t: Services Australia: aftercare or post-operative treatment

scenarios.consult: Pat, five days after you excised a lesion from his back, comes in with a red, hot, discharging wound. You assess and start antibiotics.
options: An attendance with no flag; the system will sort it
scenarios.why: Complications of the operation aren't normal aftercare. Bill the attendance and set the aftercare override, or note 'Not Normal Aftercare' (NNAC or NNA) in the service text.
scenarios.risk: Without the flag, the claim can be rejected as aftercare.

sources.t: Services Australia: aftercare or post-operative treatment

scenarios.consult: Ivy had a lesion excised by a GP in another town while on holiday. She can't get back there, so you remove her sutures.
options: No: aftercare belongs to the operator
Yes: a different practitioner can bill attendance items for the aftercare they provide
Only the original GP can bill it
Yes, the original procedure item at half fee
scenarios.why: If the patient can't return to the operating practitioner, a different practitioner can bill attendance items for the aftercare. (Specialists can't in the same situation.)
scenarios.risk: Doing it for free is generous. It's also unnecessary.

sources.t: Services Australia: aftercare or post-operative treatment

scenarios.consult: Ash, 22. Recurrent ingrown toenail. Under digital block you remove a segment of nail, remove the ungual fold, excise part of the germinal matrix, then apply phenol.
scenarios.why: 47915 is the wedge resection: nail segment, ungual fold, germinal matrix and nail bed, including phenolisation if performed. 47916 is a partial resection with phenolisation.
scenarios.risk: Adding 47916 bills the phenol twice.

scenarios.consult: Bec, 30. Partial nail avulsion of the ingrown edge with phenol to the matrix. No fold or matrix excision.
scenarios.why: Partial resection for ingrowing toenail, including phenolisation: 47916. 47915 needs the ungual fold and germinal matrix work.
scenarios.risk: 47915 for a partial resection is an over-claim.

scenarios.consult: Gwen, 66, during a 15-minute consult: three seborrhoeic keratoses and two warts frozen.
scenarios.why: Seborrhoeic keratoses (by any means), warts and molluscum, and fewer than 10 solar keratoses, are covered by attendance items.
scenarios.risk: 30192 is for 10 or more premalignant lesions. 30202 is for proven skin cancer.

sources.t: Services Australia: skin lesion and biopsy billing

scenarios.consult: You excise a 9 mm lesion (12 mm with margin) from Ross's back, clinically a BCC. Histology is pending.
scenarios.q: When and how do you bill the excision?
options: After histology: 31365 if malignant is confirmed, 31366 if not
Now, as non-malignant, and change it later
scenarios.why: Malignant skin lesion items need histological confirmation of malignancy before you bill. Any other site under 15 mm: 31365 malignant, 31366 non-malignant. Suspected-melanoma items are the exception: bill without waiting.
scenarios.risk: Billing malignant before the result is a claim you may have to repay.

sources.t: Services Australia: skin lesion and biopsy billing

scenarios.consult: You excise a lesion on Nina's back for suspected melanoma: 8 mm with margins. Specimen sent.
options: Now: suspected-melanoma items need histology sent, not the result
scenarios.why: Clinically suspected melanoma items (31377 to 31383) need histology sent, but you don't need to wait for the result. Any other body part under 15 mm: 31381.
scenarios.risk: Waiting isn't wrong, just slow. Billing it without sending the specimen is.

sources.t: Services Australia: skin lesion and biopsy billing

scenarios.consult: Hugo, 70. Two excisions on one occasion: a BCC on the nose and a lesion on the back.
scenarios.q: Which are true? (Pick all that apply.)
options: The multiple operation rule applies: 100% of the higher fee, 50% of the next
Both items must be bulk billed, or both privately billed
Note each site on the claim
Bulk bill one and privately bill the other
scenarios.why: Two or more Group T8 items on one occasion: 100%, 50%, then 25% for further items. Because the rule changes the fees, you can't split billing between them. Note each site.
scenarios.risk: Splitting T8 items under the multiple operation rule isn't allowed.

sources.t: Services Australia: billing multiple MBS items
Services Australia: skin lesion and biopsy billing

scenarios.consult: Kev, 75, has a clinically obvious superficial BCC. You curette it. No specimen sent, no histology, no specialist opinion.
options: Yes, it was clearly a BCC
No: 30196 needs histopathology, or a specialist dermatologist or plastic surgeon's confirmation with a specimen submitted
scenarios.why: 30196 and 30202 need malignancy proven by histopathology or confirmed by a specialist in dermatology or plastic surgery (30196: with a specimen submitted).
scenarios.risk: Curette first, prove later doesn't work for these items.

sources.t: Services Australia: skin lesion and biopsy billing

scenarios.consult: Lily, 27. Her implant is due. You remove it and insert a new one in the same appointment. All bulk billed.
scenarios.why: Each LARC item gets its own 35501 loading when the service is bulk billed. Removal is 30062, insertion is 14206.
scenarios.risk: Forgetting the loadings leaves 40% of two procedure fees behind.

sources.t: CERSH (Uni Melbourne): SRH MBS guide, Nov 2025 update

scenarios.consult: Noor, 32, MMM1, all bulk billed. Hormonal IUD inserted. You also take her cervical screening test (it's due) and do a urine pregnancy test in the room.
options: 23 for the separate cervical screening work
scenarios.why: Specialist sexual health guidance gives this exact pairing: 23 + 35503 + 73806 when a cervical screening or STI test is done with the insertion, plus 35501 because the LARC service is bulk billed. 14206 is for implants. 35506 is removal under general anaesthetic.
scenarios.risk: Missing the loading or the test is money left behind. 35506 isn't yours today.

sources.t: CERSH (Uni Melbourne): SRH MBS guide, Nov 2025 update

scenarios.consult: Claire, 45. Routine IUD removal in the rooms. Strings visible, out in seconds. You talk through her contraception options.
scenarios.q: How do you bill the removal?
scenarios.why: There's no MBS item for routine IUD removal: bill the attendance. 35506 is removal under general anaesthetic of a retained or embedded device. 30062 is implant removal.
scenarios.risk: 35506 for a routine removal is an over-claim with a very clear descriptor.

sources.t: CERSH (Uni Melbourne): sexual and reproductive health MBS guide, July 2026

scenarios.consult: Graham, 67, exertional chest tightness. 15-minute consult. You do a 12-lead ECG in the room and write the indication and your interpretation in the notes.
scenarios.why: Since 1 March 2026 GPs can bill 11714: a trace that informs clinical decisions during or after an attendance, with a clinical note giving the indication and interpretation. 11707 is a trace sent to a specialist or consultant physician for a formal report.
scenarios.risk: Leaving the ECG unbilled is common. So is billing 11707 for a trace you read yourself.

sources.t: MBS Online: ECG items 11707 and 11714 amended (1 March 2026)

scenarios.consult: Mabel, 80, for pre-op work-up. You do the trace and send it to the cardiologist for a formal report.
scenarios.why: 11707 is the trace only, provided to a specialist or consultant physician for a formal report. 11704 is the specialist's trace and formal report.
scenarios.risk: 11714 needs your own clinical note and interpretation.

sources.t: MBS Online: ECG items 11707 and 11714 amended (1 March 2026)
MBS Online: diagnostic items incl. 11716 (specialist or consultant physician)

scenarios.consult: Your practice owns a Holter monitor. You fit it, analyse the 24-hour recording and write the report.
options: No: 11716 is billed by a specialist or consultant physician
scenarios.why: Continuous ambulatory ECG (11716) is a specialist or consultant physician item.
scenarios.risk: A GP claim for 11716 doesn't meet the descriptor.

sources.t: MBS Online: diagnostic items incl. 11716 (specialist or consultant physician)

scenarios.consult: Ben, 52, not on treatment. Clinic BP 154/96. You arrange 24-hour ambulatory BP, interpret it, write the report and a treatment plan.
options: Yes: untreated, clinic BP in range, you interpret and report, plus a treatment plan (once in 12 months)
Only if he's had a heart health check today
scenarios.why: 11607 is 24-hour ambulatory BP for an untreated patient with clinic systolic 140 to 180 or diastolic 90 to 110 mmHg, interpreted and reported by the same practitioner, with a treatment plan. Once in 12 months.
scenarios.risk: It's not with a health assessment or care plan item, so don't bundle it into one.

scenarios.consult: Sue, 47, has her 45 to 49 health assessment (703). As part of it you organise and report a 24-hour ambulatory BP.
options: No: 11607 can't be associated with health assessment items (or 965/967)
Yes, if you bulk bill both
scenarios.why: The 11607 descriptor excludes services associated with health assessments (699, 701 to 707, 715) and care plan items including 965 and 967.
scenarios.risk: Moving it to tomorrow to dodge the rule is still associated with the assessment.

scenarios.consult: Aria, 23, suspected asthma. 12-minute consult, then pre- and post-bronchodilator spirometry with three recordings. No spirometry billed in the past year.
scenarios.why: 11505 is diagnostic spirometry, pre and post bronchodilator, once in 12 months. Spirometry minutes don't count toward the consult tier.
scenarios.risk: Counting spirometry minutes into a 36 banks time across two services.

scenarios.consult: Six months later, Aria is back for asthma review with repeat pre- and post-bronchodilator spirometry.
scenarios.why: 11505 is once in any 12 months. 11506 is the monitoring item, billable each occasion recordings are made.
scenarios.risk: A second 11505 within 12 months gets rejected.

scenarios.consult: Your practice is accredited for point-of-care testing. Rex has established type 2 diabetes. This year: two lab HbA1cs and one point-of-care HbA1c (73812). Today you'd like another point-of-care HbA1c.
options: Yes: this is his 4th HbA1c in 12 months and only his 2nd 73812
No: point-of-care HbA1c is once a year
No: lab and point-of-care can't be mixed
Yes, and a 5th next month too
scenarios.why: 73812 is max 3 in 12 months, and items 66551, 73812 and 73826 combined can't exceed 4 in 12 months. Two lab plus one point-of-care makes today the 4th: OK. A 5th wouldn't be.
scenarios.risk: Count the lab tests too. The cap is combined.

sources.t: RACGP: MBS point-of-care testing, what GPs need to know

scenarios.consult: Accredited practice. Lou, 50, high diabetes risk, never diagnosed. You'd like a point-of-care HbA1c to diagnose diabetes.
options: No: 73812 is for managing established diabetes
Yes, if the result is over 48
scenarios.why: 73812 is HbA1c in the management of established diabetes, as a point-of-care test in an accredited practice. For diagnosis, request a lab test.
scenarios.risk: A diagnostic 73812 doesn't meet the descriptor.

sources.t: RACGP: MBS point-of-care testing, what GPs need to know

scenarios.consult: Ellie, 29. You prepare her mental health treatment plan (32 minutes, no MH skills training). Separately, she has an asthma flare you assess and treat (8 minutes). Times recorded separately.
scenarios.why: Multiple services on the same day are fine when they're distinct, clinically relevant and each item's requirements are met independently, with separate time. The plan is 2700 (20 to under 40 minutes, no training); the asthma is a 23.
scenarios.risk: Unlike GP chronic condition plans, there's no blanket same-day ban here. Banking time across both is still a no.

sources.t: RACGP: MBS mental health item changes for GPs

scenarios.consult: Rita has a GPCCMP. Today you do her 967 review. Separately, the practice nurse dresses her leg ulcer, consistent with the plan.
scenarios.q: Can the nurse's service be billed as 10997?
options: Possibly: co-claiming may be appropriate where the nurse's service is separate from, but consistent with, the plan review
Only if the GP is in the room
scenarios.why: 10997 is for ongoing care consistent with the plan, between reviews. Co-claiming it with a planning or review item may be appropriate where the nurse's work is separate from the plan development or review.
scenarios.risk: The 23 on top of 967 is the trap here, not the nurse.

scenarios.consult: The practice nurse spends 20 minutes collecting information and measurements to help you prepare Neil's GPCCMP (965).
scenarios.q: Can the nurse's time be billed as 10997?
options: No: 10997 can't be used for help preparing a GPCCMP
Yes, if the 965 is bulk billed
scenarios.why: 10997 can't be used for a nurse's assistance with preparing a GPCCMP. 965 is a complete service and the only item for preparing the plan.
scenarios.risk: Splitting plan preparation into 965 + 10997 is double-dipping on one service.

scenarios.consult: Walk-in: the nurse dresses a graze for Ken, who has no GPCCMP or multidisciplinary care plan. You don't see him.
options: No: 10997 is for patients with a GPCCMP or multidisciplinary care plan
Yes, as a 23 under your provider number
scenarios.why: 10997 (and video 93201, phone 93203) covers up to 5 services a calendar year for patients with a GPCCMP or multidisciplinary care plan.
scenarios.risk: A 23 for a service you didn't personally provide is a much bigger problem.

scenarios.consult: Elsie, 78. 75+ health assessment (50 minutes). She also has a new productive cough and fever that needs managing today (10 minutes, recorded separately).
scenarios.q: Can you bill an attendance as well as the health assessment?
options: Yes: a separate problem that needs managing, with each item's time met separately
Yes, and count the 50 minutes toward both
Only if she comes back tomorrow
scenarios.why: Don't add a consult to a health assessment unless it's clinically necessary, i.e. a problem needing separate management. Each item's time must be separately met, and time can't be counted twice.
scenarios.risk: Routine add-on consults with health assessments are what PSR looks for.

scenarios.consult: For Fred's 45 to 49 health assessment, the nurse spends 25 minutes collecting history and measurements; you spend 20 minutes on examination, plan and advice.
scenarios.q: Can you bill a nurse item for the nurse's part?
options: No: nurse time assisting a health assessment goes only to the assessment item
Yes, if the nurse writes separate notes
scenarios.why: Practice nurses can assist with health assessments, but that time goes only to the health assessment item. Delegation shouldn't inflate the item either.
scenarios.risk: PSR has flagged assessments that were mostly nurse data collection with little GP input.

scenarios.consult: Your practice manager suggests booking every health assessment with a GPCCMP straight after, same day, 'for efficiency'.
options: Only when both are clinically relevant, separate and distinct; it shouldn't be routine
scenarios.why: A health assessment and care plan can be claimed the same day only if both are clinically relevant, separate and distinct, and each item's requirements are met. A plan would usually follow an assessment that finds a chronic condition.
scenarios.risk: A routine pairing is exactly the kind of pattern that gets reviewed.

scenarios.consult: Jill, 47, eligible for a heart health check (699) and a 45 to 49 health assessment, both today.
options: Heart health check first, then the 45 to 49 assessment
They can't be on the same day
scenarios.why: 699 can't be claimed after another health assessment in the previous 12 months, but a standard assessment can follow a 699. On the same day it's only permissible if the standard assessment comes after the heart health check.
scenarios.risk: Get the order wrong and the 699 gets knocked back.

scenarios.consult: Ruby, 30, period late, home test positive. History and exam (8 minutes), urine pregnancy test in the room, confirmed. Then 12 minutes of antenatal care: dates, folic acid, bloods.
scenarios.why: The PHN worked example: 23 for the initial history and exam, 73806 for the in-room urine pregnancy test, then 16500 for antenatal care of the confirmed pregnancy. Record times.
scenarios.risk: Dropping 73806 leaves the test you did unbilled.

sources.t: CESPHN: antenatal and pregnancy MBS items (Aug 2026)

scenarios.consult: Tash, 6 weeks after giving birth. 25 minutes: recovery, feeding, contraception, mood screening.
scenarios.why: 16407 is the postnatal attendance 4 to 8 weeks after birth, at least 20 minutes, including a mental health assessment. 16408 is 1 to 4 weeks after a private admission. 16500 is antenatal.
scenarios.risk: Using 23 here undersells a specific, better-fitting item.

sources.t: CERSH (Uni Melbourne): sexual and reproductive health MBS guide, July 2026
CESPHN: antenatal and pregnancy MBS items (Aug 2026)

scenarios.consult: You've already claimed 16590 for Grace's pregnancy. At 34 weeks you do her shared-care management visit.
options: No: only one of 16590 or 16591 per pregnancy
Yes, if it's a different GP
scenarios.why: 16591 isn't claimable if 16590 has been provided for the same pregnancy, and vice versa.
scenarios.risk: The second one gets rejected.

sources.t: CESPHN: antenatal and pregnancy MBS items (Aug 2026)

scenarios.consult: Cal, 40, wants a privately bought flu vaccine. You also review his reflux. 10 minutes.
options: An attendance item (23); the vaccine itself isn't billable to Medicare
Nothing: vaccines are never Medicare services
scenarios.why: There's no MBS item for the vaccine. When you immunise, you can usually bill an attendance item, unless other funding covers giving it.
scenarios.risk: Medicare can't pay for the vaccine product itself.

sources.t: Services Australia: MBS billing for immunisations

scenarios.consult: You give a COVID-19 vaccine to an eligible patient after assessing suitability.
scenarios.why: The COVID-19 vaccine suitability items (including 93644 to 93656, 10660 and 10661) ceased on 1 July 2025. Use the relevant attendance item. Incentives apply if bulk billed.
scenarios.risk: Billing a ceased item gets rejected.

sources.t: CESPHN: COVID-19 vaccine support items ceased 1 July 2025
Services Australia: MBS billing for immunisations

scenarios.consult: Ivy, 26, eligible for MBS telehealth, has a routine antenatal review by video.
scenarios.why: 16500's telehealth equivalents: video 91853, phone 91858.
scenarios.risk: Billing a face-to-face item for a video consult is a mismatch.

sources.t: CERSH (Uni Melbourne): sexual and reproductive health MBS guide, July 2026

scenarios.consult: On a video call, Zoe asks you to bill her IUD check and a 'remote' implant removal next week as telehealth items.
options: Yes, the check and the removal
scenarios.why: LARC procedure items have no telehealth equivalents. The video consult itself can be a telehealth attendance.
scenarios.risk: You'd need very long arms.

sources.t: CERSH (Uni Melbourne): sexual and reproductive health MBS guide, July 2026

coclaims.pair: Level B to E attendance (23, 36, 44, 123) + triple incentive
coclaims.cond: Bulk billed, any Medicare-eligible patient since 1 Nov 2025. MMM1: 75870. The incentive number changes with the Modified Monash category.

sources.t: MBS Online: BBI changes factsheet (1 Nov 2025)

coclaims.cond: Level A gets the single incentive (10990 in MMM1), not the triple.

sources.t: MBS Online: Supporting bulk billing in general practice factsheet
